item.description:
I own Rayman Legends on six platforms. The game, a 2D platformer that launched back in 2013, initially released onto the PS3, Xbox 360, PC, Wii U and PS Vita. A year later, it came to Xbox One and PS4. Fast-forward three years and it's on Switch, and then in 2021 it came to Stadia, too. It's been around the block a few times then, and I've gone with it each time - I have 1000Gs and a Platinum trophy for it. It's just a very, very good game.
But what makes it so enduring? It's the creativity oozing out of every pore. The simple run-and-jump platforming feels excellent in your hands, the animations that back it up are luscious and fun, and the music and sound design treads that precarious line between utterly charming and slightly vexing. As a game, it's imaginative and generous - a kind-hearted hug that encourages you to move out of deceptively simple normal levels into time trials, assault courses, and gauntlets in a warm and friendly way.
Its musical levels - famous gibberish versions of "Black Betty", "Eye of the Tiger", and "Woo-Hoo" - were iconic from launch, and have become crystallised as a highlight of the entire Rayman oeuvre ever since. They encapsulate everything about the playful, slightly silly joy of Rayman: unlikely rhythm-action sections of mild platforming peril. Not too hard, not too easy. As concerned with titillating you as it is with making you smile. When Ubisoft announced Rayman Legends Retold, I was worried that whatever work the twinned studios of Ubi Montpellier and Milan would do would somehow undo whatever magic was woven into these levels 13 years ago - moving from pure 2D to 2.5D, after all, is enough to break the illusion alone.
My fears were unfounded, though. After playing a good three hours of the game - including one old music level and one new one - I realised the team behind Retold must hold the original game in as much esteem as I do; understanding that delicate balance between goofy fun and platforming perfection is an important line to toe. An interview after my preview confirmed my suspicions.
"It has been one of the best experiences of my life, to be honest," says Marco Renso, animation and realisation director on Rayman Legends Retold at Ubisoft Milan, when I ask him about working on these new musical levels. "As a game dev, I've always loved musical levels, but working on new ones… it doesn't happen often that you get to work on something so creative and enjoyable. Honestly, from the start of the process - coming up with the ideas - to finishing it off with art, music, animation and everything else. Making it all come together is like conducting a composition yourself; every asset, every beat, it has to work together to create a rhythm and pacing experience. It's one of the most creative environments possible, basically."
"I will just add to what Marco said, the toughest part has been choosing the tracks," laughs Loïc Gounon, brand producer at Ubisoft Montpellier, "because there's so many options early on. But when it comes to the selection of tracks, we wanted to have a bit more choice, you know? We wanted more tracks for everyone. Before, it was not all tracks that we all liked, I would say - we were in a bit of a rush and said 'OK, let's put that in the game'. This time, I think we tried to have a bit more thought about trying to please more people.. that doesn't mean that we'll do only very trendy types of track, for example. We really want something for everyone."
Gounon goes on to explain that the team's biggest wish when it comes to these new tracks is that "older folks and younger folks" will both appreciate the new music that has been added to the game because, after all, music is transgenerational. "It can be a kid saying to his dad 'oh, that's my track' or the opposite, right? A dad telling his kid, 'oh, you know, I grew up with this song'. You get to enjoy it together."
So far, we only know about two new musical levels in the game. Firstly, a song inspired by the Macarena (above) where, at one point in the madcap dash through a Mexican wrestling rink-cum-kitchen, you get to see the luchador boss you'll fight in a later stage doing the iconic Macarena dance. Great, no notes. Secondly, there's one inspired by U Can't Touch This by MC Hammer. These will stand alongside the six original songs to make "a dozen" musical levels in the game, all-in-all. So, by my count, that's another four unaccounted for... what could they be?
Interestingly, the gameplay feels exactly the same as the original games - it'd be heresy if it felt any different, we all know how that worked out for Crash Bandicoot. This is because the engine powering the physics, gameplay mechanics, collision and so on - UbiArt Framework - is running within another engine that's handling the visuals, audio, and rendering. It's like a "Russian doll", Gounon laughs. "It's still running as it was the first time, you know, but re-rendered more beautifully!"
Renso adds that moving the game from 2D to 2.5D was also an opportunity to "play with depth, with the size of the characters, with the storytelling of [the game],". This led to new opportunities when it came to the new levels the teams added to Retold, too. "One example is the zip line that you see in several musical levels," he explains. "At some points, a big and long zip line can be a moment where you don't need a gameplay input; you can just look at something. So maybe that's a good moment [to bend the camera] and let you enjoy something in the background." You can see this in the video above; when the luchador starts dancing, we're given time to collect ourselves, enjoy the nonsense of it all, before being thrown back into the action.
"Rayman is not Hollow Knight," says Gounon, when I ask about balancing the difficulty the series is known for (Rayman on the PS1 is still hard as nails in 2026) with the clear intention the devs have of getting parents to play this with their kids. "But still, there is a DNA of die-and-retry platforming here. So it's not, like, a hyper-casual platformer, but it's also not the most hardcore Metroidvania, either. So that's where we are with Rayman: attracting people that like a challenge, but also like to finish the story. We are platforming fans that like to be tested. And even if we play with our kids, we want them to also enjoy that, too."
Gounon has said in a previous interview that Ubisoft sees Rayman Legends Retold as a 'new starting point' for Rayman. But, in chatting to him about this game, I can see that Retold is more than just a cynical cash-in for a platforming mascot - this is a personal project for him. "I'm a bit like you, Dom," he tells me. "I played the first Rayman on my PS1, as a launch title. So I have a long history with Rayman that started when I was 12 or 13 years old. I played in Rayman 2 before joining Ubisoft, and it was one of the reasons why I joined the company. Then, I worked on a version of Rayman 4 in 2006 with Michel Ancel, and his team that became Raving Rabbids (a franchise I handled for a couple of years). Then we had another run at Rayman 4 - that became Origins - and it all came back to Montpellier.
"It's really cool to reconnect with the characters of the world [with Retold], and part of what we are doing in world building, storytelling, emotion… It's all making us think about what will come next. This isn't just a one-shot remake; it's part of a much bigger picture that we hope is going to capture original fans, but also their kids, and introduce them to this wonderful world."
We learned last week that Ubisoft has delayed Rayman Legends Retold in order to "make sure every detail gets the care it deserves", moving the release date from 1st October to 3rd December. I hope this means the game launches into a slightly less crowded world; one that is ready to take Rayman's floating hand once again and experience the light-hearted joy of his weird little universe. Lord knows we'll probably need it after the gritty realism of that other big game launching in November, right?

item.title: Following reports that further job cuts were imminent at Xbox, Microsoft has confirmed more sweeping changes as its major restructuring continues. As a result, some Xbox studios will combine, others are set for closure, and 268 more layoffs have been announced. Read more
item.description:
Following reports that further job cuts were imminent at Xbox, Microsoft has confirmed more sweeping changes as its major restructuring continues. As a result, some Xbox studios will combine, others are set for closure, and 268 more layoffs have been announced.
In July, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced job cuts affecting 3,200 employees as part of what she called the "most significant" restructuring the company had ever undertaken. 1,600 of those layoffs were effective immediately, while some first-pary studios, including Double Fine and Compulsion Games, were permitted to go independent again.
And with the threat of 1,600 more cuts hanging over the heads of remaining employees, Sharma has swung the axe again. This time, layoffs will affect 268 employees across Halo Studios, other unspecified first-party studios, and members of Xbox Game Studios' "management and central functions layer".
As part of the latest changes, many Xbox studios have undergone reorganisation. In a note to employees shared on the Xbox blog, Xbox executive vice president and chief content officer Matt Booty explained that Sea of Thieves developer Rare and Age of Empires/Mythology studio World's Edge now fall within Activision's remit, Playground and Turn 10 will join together to focus on Forza and Fable, and Bethesda will oversee Obsidian, which continues to work on its current projects including Grounded, and will collaborate with Bethesda Game Studios on a new Fallout project.
Additionally, the next Halo game will be developed by Activision, led by a "new, purpose-built team" away from Call of Duty. A "small" remaining team at Halo Studios will support "the Halo community and games in-market".
Booty said these latest changes were designed to "strengthen our franchises and games by operating fewer business units, aligning groups that already work closely together, and focusing our publishing expertise." He also offered an update on two first-party studios whose fates have remained in limbo following July's sweeping job cuts, and it's bad news.
Hellblade developer Ninja Theory is now facing "proposed closure" after two separate agreements fell through, and Microsoft is beginning consultation with employees as it continues to explore "other paths forward". Consultation with Arkane, the studio behind the likes of Dishonored and Deathloop, "remains underway and is expected to continue through the end of the year."
Today's news - which is said to bring Microsoft "roughly three-quarters of the way through previously announced restructuring" - marks more losses following July's devastating job cuts, and suggests more than 1,300 employees could still be facing layoffs before the process is through.

item.title: Ninja Theory - developer of the Hellblade series of games, Enslaved: Odyssey to the West, DmC: Devil May Cry, and Heavenly Sword - is entering consultation in preperation for the studio's closure as part of today's sweeping Xbox cuts and layoffs. Read more
item.description:
Ninja Theory - developer of the Hellblade series of games, Enslaved: Odyssey to the West, DmC: Devil May Cry, and Heavenly Sword - is entering consultation in preperation for the studio's closure as part of today's sweeping Xbox cuts and layoffs.
Announced by a new Xbox Wire blog post penned by Xbox chief content officer Matt Booty, Ninja Theory employees and Xbox will begin a consultation process as the studio looks to head towards a closure.
The blog post reads: "Unfortunately, two separate agreements for Ninja Theory fell through. We will now begin consultation with employees on a proposed closure while continuing to explore other paths forward."
Ninja Theory had seemed safe during Xbox's initial wave of job and studio cuts in July, having apparently entered a partnership to an unnamed company. But that seems to have changed, leaving Ninja Theory without an owner and unable to continue operation.
The studio was developing Senua, a new entry in the studios' Hellblade action adventure series - a game only announced in June as part of an Xbox Games Showcase. Senua was said to be a larger, "more expansive" game compared to previous entries in the series. Within a month of its reveal Ninja Theory was put up for sale by Microsoft.
The blog post ends with the following: "Today, our focus should be on supporting those affected and treating one another with care and respect. I will spend time with our studios over the next week. At our October 6 town hall, we will come together as an All-Xbox team to reflect on our progress and look ahead to one of the strongest game lineups in our history."
Ninja Theory was known for some solid releases over the years. Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice was a stunning premiere for the series, and the studio released some interesting games like Disney Infinity: 3.0, Bleeding Edge, and Dexed.
A previous version of this article had the headline "Hellblade developer Ninja Theory to be shut down in new wave of Xbox cuts, as two separate agreements collapse". The announcement from Xbox says consultation on a "proposed closure" has begun while other options are explored. Eurogamer apologises for this error.

item.title: Halo Studios (formerly 343 Industries) won't develop the next mainline Halo game because it's being what sounds like drastically reduced in size. Microsoft has instead given development duty to Activision, which is making "a new purpose-built team" separate to Call of Duty to make it. Read more
item.description:
Halo Studios (formerly 343 Industries) won't develop the next mainline Halo game because it's being what sounds like drastically reduced in size. Microsoft has instead given development duty to Activision, which is making "a new purpose-built team" separate to Call of Duty to make it.
"We are eliminating 268 roles across Halo Studios, other first-party studios, and the XGS management and central functions layer," Xbox Studios boss Matt Booty wrote in a statement. "Activision will also be developing the next Halo title, led by a new, purpose-built team that is separate from ongoing development and plans for Call of Duty. A small team at Halo Studios will continue supporting the Halo community and games in-market," Booty wrote.
In a statement provided to Kotaku, Activision president Rob Kostich said: "We're thrilled to welcome Halo, Rare, and World's Edge to Activision." (Rare is also going to Activision.) "It's an honor and a responsibility that we do not take lightly. These teams and their games have inspired fans around the world for decades.
"For Halo, our goal is clear: make the greatest Halo game ever, worthy of its universe and legacy, while staying true to what made players love it in the first place. It is a bold ambition, one that this franchise deserves. We have already begun assembling a purpose-built team, unique in capability and talent, ready and excited to deliver this next chapter with the community."
The news arrives as part of another wave of major Microsoft Xbox restructuring, which has seen hundreds more people lose their jobs, British studio Ninja Theory close, and studios like Obsidian and Rare, as mentioned, consolidated into being controlled by others.
The Halo series, originated by Bungie, was overseen by 343 Industries/Halo Studios ever since Bungie bought its independence from Microsoft in 2007. Halo Studios (it rebranded in 2024) made a number of mainline Halo games, including 2012's Halo 4, 2015's Halo 5: Guardians, 2021's Halo Infinite, and most recently the reboot of Halo 1, Halo: Campaign Evolved.
Halo Studios also collaborated on every other Halo project, including 2014's Halo: The Master Chief Collection and the Halo Wars games. This move by Microsoft is, then, a significant departure for the Halo series.

item.title: Sony appears to be testing a new PlayStation rewards programme. A number of posts on social media and Reddit have recently appeared showing that purchasing certain games from the PlayStation Store now comes with an associated wallet credit bonus. Read more
item.description:
Sony appears to be testing a new PlayStation rewards programme. A number of posts on social media and Reddit have recently appeared showing that purchasing certain games from the PlayStation Store now comes with an associated wallet credit bonus.
A post from Reddit user JannJans ( spotted by PlayStation Lifestyle) shows wallet credit bonuses for both versions of The Blood of Dawnwalker on their US version of the PlayStation Store. Both the game's Standard and Eclipse editions show a message that says "includes wallet credit", with an offer end-date of 29th September.
"I was deciding between Dragon's Dogma 2 and Blood of Dawnwalker and noticed a special offer with the latter," the Reddit user wrote. Sure enough, after purchasing the game, $10 was sent to their PS Store Wallet.
Other users reported seeing similar messages, including outside of the US. The offer doesn't appear to be limited to The Blood of Dawnwalker, either, with some reportedly seeing it attached to Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy, Star Wars Zero Company and Halloween: The game - all of them recent releases.
While there's no direct indication of the bonus being part of a larger rewards scheme, PlayStation Lifestyle did also uncover a PlayStation Store app called Wallet Credits in February, so the two could be connected.
The idea of offering store credit with certain purchases obviously isn't new - it's used around the world in many stores. Console competitor Microsoft has used this approach for years on the Xbox Store; we recently saw Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 pre-orders offering a $5 / £4 credit for a limited time.
As to why the offer is available to some players but not others, we don't know, but it could be related to PlayStation's experimentation with dynamic pricing, which allows it to offer games at different prices for different customers, based on its assessment of the likelihood of them buying it.
It's also possible this is part of a larger rewards or loyalty programme Sony is working on, and perhaps preparing to announce, and that the players experiencing it happen to be at a tier designated to receive it.

item.title: UPDATE 4PM BST: Game Developer has reportedly seen an email Blizzard sent to employees that indicates it - or at least the World of Warcraft department - isn't affected by "today's announcements". An Xbox representative apparently verified the email's legitimacy. Read more
item.description:
UPDATE 4PM BST: Game Developer has reportedly seen an email Blizzard sent to employees that indicates it - or at least the World of Warcraft department - isn't affected by "today's announcements". An Xbox representative apparently verified the email's legitimacy.
UPDATE 3.30PM BST: Blizzard does not appear to be included in the latest wave of Xbox layoffs, which have seen 268 job losses and studios either closed, drastically downsized, or merged with other studios.
As part of the cuts, British studio Ninja Theory has closed, Halo Studios has been downsized and Halo development handed to Activision, Obsidian has become a part of Bethesda, and Playground and Turn 10 have come together as one studio. Rare is also now a part of Activision.
ORIGINAL STORY 1PM BST: A week after an announcement-laden BlizzCon 2026, and days after what appears to be an enormously popular beta for World of Warcraft: Forever, cuts at Blizzard by Xbox are said to be "imminent".
Word comes from Bloomberg reporter Jason Schreier, who previously wrote a detailed book about Blizzard's history based on numerous contacts there. Speaking in a recent episode of the 8-4 podcast (via Resetera), Schreier said: "To your point: yes the Blizzard layoffs are coming and imminent."
Schreier was answering a question from former Polygon journalist Mike McWhertor about whether Blizzard announced so many new games at BlizzCon 2026 because Xbox cuts were looming. Blizzard unveiled Diablo 5, a new StarCraft open-world shooter, a new World of Warcraft game, a new Warcraft 3 campaign, and other, smaller things. Some of these games had release dates as far away as 2030, in Diablo 5's case.
Schreier, however, dismissed the notion that this was a cuts-related play, saying he believed Blizzard planned its BlizzCon showing a year in advance. "Pretty sure they were planning on announcing StarCraft there before Asha Sharma even took over," he said.
As for the distant release dates, he said Blizzard always internally planned things far in advance, but just didn't communicate those targets with the public. "This is them saying we are going to actually ship when we say we're going to ship rather than slipping," he said.
"Because one of the major things that has happened to Blizzard over the last few years, and one of the reasons they had so many problems with Activision, is that they promised that Diablo 4 and Overwatch 2 were both going to come out in certain timeframes and then both of those games kept slipping, which led to Bobby Kotick cracking the whip, cutting costs there, causing them all sorts of problems. So I think this is them trying to enact some discipline there."
Schreier also believes that newish Blizzard president Johanna Faries has "a lot of autonomy on this stuff", and insisted "this is not a Microsoft thing", when referring to the BlizzCon announcements. Therefore, he added: "I don't think this was because of [impending cuts]. The layoffs started in July, people found out about them in June; all this BlizzCon stuff was prepared way before that."
Schreier's mention of "imminent" Blizzard cuts is amplified by reports from this morning that a second wave of Xbox cuts is expected this week. Microsoft, remember, announced its intention to cut 3200 jobs from the Xbox division earlier this year, immediately cutting 1600 roles and earmarking 1600 to be cut thereafter. Blizzard seemed to emerge unscathed from the first round of layoffs, and was even mentioned as Xbox's "top performing" studio in the aftermath, but it may not have escaped the cuts entirely.

item.title: We now have even more confirmation a new Injustice game is in development. Following last week's playtest leak, information has emerged that sheds more light on the upcoming DC fighting game. Read more
item.description:
We now have even more confirmation a new Injustice game is in development. Following last week's playtest leak, information has emerged that sheds more light on the upcoming DC fighting game.
Two characters from the game's roster of fighters have appeared on the resume of a stunt worker who previously worked with developer NetherRealm. As reported by MP1st, the resume for Mackensi Emory included direct references to Injustice 3, though it has since been updated to remove all mention of the game.
The stunt worker was part of motion capture sessions for Injustice 3, specifically portraying the characters Supergirl and Batwoman. Supergirl's appearance is expected, given her central role in Injustice 2's narrative, but Batwoman is a surprise.
Not only will this be Batwoman's first appearance in an Injustice game, but her arrival is all the more notable because in the world of Injustice, she's dead; at least, Batwoman is dead according to the official comic books, which are considered canon. Indeed, as MP1st points out, the comics and the games frequently reference one another so it would be strange for the third game to break from that continuity.
How could this work? Well, a dead comic book character revival isn't impossible in the world of superheros, and it's possible a different person could have taken up Batwoman's mantle - a common way for comic books to bring a character back.
It's also worth noting that the upcoming game may not be a continuation of the events of the two prior games at all, and could act as a timeline reset, featuring new versions of the iconic DC characters.
Beyond that, Emory's resume also confirmed animator and stunt coordinator Jake Huang's involvement in the project, who previously worked with NetherRealm on Mortal Kombat 1.
Injustice 3 hasn't been announced yet and there's no known release date, but given NetherRealm's previous development pacing, we expect a new Injustice game could arrive in 2027 (the last NR game being 2023's MK1). Would a reveal at December's Game Awards make sense, in this case? We shall wait and see.

item.title: World of Warcraft: Forever's beta is here, offering us our first look at WoW's reimagined vanilla or classic experience, and already it's proving extremely popular. But there are points of contention, one being whether the new Skyborne race's starting zone fits tonally with original-race zones. Read more
item.description:
World of Warcraft: Forever's beta is here, offering us our first look at WoW's reimagined vanilla or classic experience, and already it's proving extremely popular. But there are points of contention, one being whether the new Skyborne race's starting zone fits tonally with original-race zones.
Part of the pitch for WoW Forever, made at BlizzCon recently, was any new stories added to the vanilla or classic experience would remain grounded within the established stakes or tone of original World of Warcraft. However, the introduction of the Skyborne elves and the narrative established in their starting zone have caused some concerns.
At BlizzCon, the approach to updating World of Warcraft in Forever was labelled as "found photographs", the idea being that anything new added to the game could have feasibly been present within Classic WoW. But some believe the major Skyborne starting questline pushes back against that premise. Spoilers for the Skyborne levelling zone ahead, heads up.
To sum it up briefly, the island the Skyborne call home was lifted into and hidden within the elemental plane of wind - known as Skywall - many years ago. And the conclusion of the starting zone questline has you watch while an elemental lord is summoned - one of the underlings of Al'Akir, the big nasty ruler of Skywall - to tell you he'll return to take over the place in the future.
This immediately goes against the strategy of keeping things within Classic's scope. Elemental lords are not seen in Classic WoW until players confront fire lord Ragnaros in a level 60 raid in Molten Core. But here, you're thrust into a confrontation with one before you hit level 15. Compare that with the human starting zone, which ends with a confrontation with Hogger, a chieftain of a nasty pack of gnolls, and you see the difference.
"On Zephras Isle [the Skyborne island] you, together with the leaders of your people, face a raid-level threat at the top of the spire, through a scripted event with bountiful exposition text, and the leaders of the Kirin Tor and the Earthen Ring show up to fend off this raid boss," wrote user OccasionallyRhyming on the Classic WoW Reddit. "If it was not for your actions on Zephras Isle, your people would be doomed.
"I'm okay with ignoring the Skyborne and enjoying the rest of the game, but everything about their addition just screams warning about how Blizzard will approach future content."
This fear of Skyborne-related grandeur was shared by other players, who responded with their own concerns. "Meanwhile I'm over here pilfering Tirisfal pumpkins and picking Gloomweed," wrote -Necron-Overlord-. Another user, Altmly, said: "Agreed, Blizzard is incapable of writing ordinary stories that have weight without involving some world saving, universe defining, celebrity creating mumbo jumbo bullcrap."
However, it's worth noting that elsewhere in the game, new quests are down to earth. Players have been picking up rocks off the ground in Orgrimmar or finding lost loved ones in new dungeons, and these seem to have gone down well. It's just the inclusion of the Skyborne questline that appears to have jarred.
Ultimately, the fuller picture of Blizzard's "Lost Photographs" approach will only be available once WoW Forever game releases in full on 4th November. For now, players remain curious to see just how successful a modern development team will be at capturing the spirit of a decades' old adventure.

item.title: Xbox is reportedly preparing to lay off hundreds more people this week as the company plans to consolidate several of its studios. Read more
item.description:
Xbox is reportedly preparing to lay off hundreds more people this week as the company plans to consolidate several of its studios.
The news comes from an exclusive report on The Information, which cites a source briefed about Microsoft's plans. The report does not say which of Xbox's many studios are affected and which are being consolidated.
If correct, this would be the second wave of Xbox layoffs this year, following major restructuring in July that resulted in 1,600 job cuts. This is part of Xbox CEO Asha Sharma's plan to "reset" Microsoft's gaming division and return it to profitability. When those cuts were announced, Sharma also said the company intended to cut a further 1,600 jobs before a year had passed (taking us to next summer, approximately). These reported layoffs could be that second wave.
July's layoffs saw cuts across almost the entirety of Xbox's studio portfolio, though some teams were more affected than others. Xbox also shed a handful of studios, with some of those, such as Double Fine Productions and Compulsion Games, buying back their independence. Other studios, such as Ninja Theory and State of Decay maker Undead Labs, were instead sold to as-yet unnamed buyers, and Dishonored studio Arkane Lyon is undergoing consultation, and its fate remains unknown.
Sharma's plan is for Xbox to focus on making games in its biggest franchises, such as The Elder Scrolls and Fallout. But the cuts impacted Fallout and Elder Scrolls maker Bethesda too, and Elder Scrolls Online developer Zenimax Online. Doom and Quake maker id Software was also heavily impacted.
As a result, morale was reportedly low at Xbox following July's cuts and it's not likely to get better this week, should the layoffs occur.

item.title: Ahead of the bottomless GTA 6 mods we'll surely get whenever the crime epic finally comes to PC, Rockstar Games has imposed new restrictions on the modding community and, boy, they are tight. Read more
item.description:
Ahead of the bottomless GTA 6 mods we'll surely get whenever the crime epic finally comes to PC, Rockstar Games has imposed new restrictions on the modding community and, boy, they are tight.
"Rockstar Games is the home of the Grand Theft Auto and Red Dead Redemption series, and other titles," the studio reminds us in its mod guidelines, which were updated earlier this month and spread around the internet more recently. "To maintain a fun, creative, and welcoming place for players and content creators, we encourage everyone to keep the following in mind."
The developer's first rule is to "respect our games." That means modders can no longer "expand or modify Rockstar Games' official storylines, plots, missions, characters, or other elements of our established continuity." Modders are also not allowed to combine maps or assets or characters from one Rockstar game with another - Arthur Morgan appearing in Vice City is probably a no-no, then.
"Multiplayer modding is limited to Rockstar Games' official licensed Creator Platform or else as otherwise licensed directly by Rockstar Games," it added. "Do not modify our games to operate on consoles, hardware devices, or other platforms where they have not been officially released by Rockstar Games."
While these guidelines feel like Rockstar is perhaps holding too tight a leash, some of its points are otherwise pretty reasonable. Rockstar won't "tolerate abuse, bullying, threats, or harassment of any kind," for example - fair enough - and mods can't be monetised "unless permitted via Rockstar Games' official Creator Platform."
The full list draws a pretty strict line in the sand, and I can't imagine we'll see nearly the same amount of zany mods for GTA 6 as we have for GTA 5 as a result.
Elsewhere, Twitch's CEO recently let slip that GTA 6 Online might launch next year instead. Rockstar also properly announced its own GTA Online RP server a few weeks ago, years after trying to bury (and then acquiring) the modding team behind it.

item.title: Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire might join their handheld third-generation siblings on a journey to the Nintendo Switch - at least, that's what fans think after an official channel posted what looks like a HD version of the classic games that are definitely not running on a Game Boy Advance. Read more
item.description:
Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire might join their handheld third-generation siblings on a journey to the Nintendo Switch - at least, that's what fans think after an official channel posted what looks like a HD version of the classic games that are definitely not running on a Game Boy Advance.
Earlier today, an official Pokémon social media account shared a 30-second, suspiciously crisp clip of Wingull, the player-controlled trainer and Mr. Briney chasing each other around in Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire.
The Pokémon official account has posted a clip of Pokémon Ruby/Sapphire being played on an unknown emulator 🤔 https://t.co/aHDTy1F2Dl
Alarm bells immediately went off in the brains of many Pokémon fans. "This is an official account tweeting out high-res gameplay from Pokemon Ruby/Sapphire," YouTuber That Bald Gamer tweeted. "Since these graphics aren't possible on their original official hardware, I'd say this essentially means Pokemon Ruby/Sapphire ports are coming to the Nintendo Switch in some fashion."
Adding more fuel to the fire is the fact that Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 recordings automatically captures footage from the last 30 seconds of gameplay, which is exactly how long the video above lasts. And official channels normally don't use emulated versions of older Pokémon games in promotional clips - the video above is almost definitely not from the games' original 2002 release.
As noted by Kotaku, dataminers found that this year's Nintendo Switch ports of Pokémon FireRed and LeafGreen seemingly included ROM support for all third-gen mainline games too, including Sapphire, Ruby and the expanded Emerald. This certainly doesn't outright confirm that HD Ruby and Sapphire ports are on the way, but it does suggest some work has already been done in that direction.
Pokemon FireRed and LeafGreen's Switch re-releases were also immediate best-sellers on the system, selling upwards of 4m units in their first six weeks alone. Not bad for two-decade-old remakes, eh? I imagine another opportunity to explore Hoenn would receive just as warm a welcome, if the price is right.

item.title: Bungie's been having a tough time these past few years, but the studio's new leadership is making big promises. Starting with Destiny 2 - the devs will start to let some of the game's older campaigns and raids out of the vault, while trying to build a future for the popular MMO-FPS hybrid. And, while Marathon hasn't courted enough players yet, the studio's still working to improve the extraction shooter. Read more
item.description:
Bungie's been having a tough time these past few years, but the studio's new leadership is making big promises. Starting with Destiny 2 - the devs will start to let some of the game's older campaigns and raids out of the vault, while trying to build a future for the popular MMO-FPS hybrid. And, while Marathon hasn't courted enough players yet, the studio's still working to improve the extraction shooter.
"Bungie has been creating games for over 30 years and we have welcomed the communities that have formed around them. Over the last few years, we lost sight of that, and there have been real consequences. We lost trust, we lost incredible colleagues, and we lost sight of what we should be prioritizing most, our players," studio head Poria Torkan and head of product Josh Deane said in today's online statement. The duo then acknowledged fans probably won't start trusting "what we say today," but they're making moves to improve both Destiny and Marathon, regardless.
For context, earlier this year, Bungie laid off at least 290 employees shortly after waving goodbye to Destiny 2 with a final update. The studio's Marathon reboot hasn't been popular enough to fill the hole left by Destiny's absence, either. At the time, reports claimed there were no Destiny-related projects in active development, Destiny 3 included.
No matter. "Destiny is foundational to Bungie's future," the studio added. "We have more stories to tell, new worlds to build, but we have to do it right and give our teams the time they need to do justice to this amazing universe. All of this is to say, we are not done with Destiny."
Bungie doesn't have any new games to reveal right now, but it's starting by un-vaulting a bunch of Destiny 2 campaigns, locations and raids that were previously locked away. All players will apparently have access to those un-vaulted goodies in the coming months - Bungie still needs to tweak lighting, combat encounters and other systems to make sure "returning content meets the stability and gameplay standards of Destiny 2 today."
As for Marathon, the ultra-stylish extraction shooter "did not reach as many players as we had hoped, and we also know and understand that the game needs to evolve." Bungie plans to keep expanding upon what makes Marathon good already, according to the studio leadership, but also "evolve it beyond the genre constraints we placed on it." The previously revealed permanent PvE mode and social space coming in December should help broaden the sci-fi shooter's appeal outside of players who are only into sweaty, risk-it-all skirmishes above all else, at least.

item.title: Speaking to Eurogamer, The Blood of Dawnwalker game director Konrad Tomaszkiewicz has discussed several game improvements coming in a "big patch" currently scheduled for early October - including a brand new difficulty option, combat targeting changes, and making it easier to escape from battles by running away. Read more
item.description:
Speaking to Eurogamer, The Blood of Dawnwalker game director Konrad Tomaszkiewicz has discussed several game improvements coming in a "big patch" currently scheduled for early October - including a brand new difficulty option, combat targeting changes, and making it easier to escape from battles by running away.
Tomaszkiewicz also told me in an interview that the studio is exploring a New Game Plus mode - "Yes, we are," he said smiling but not saying anything more - and potentially adding new enemies to improve variety. "There is a chance but I don't want to speak about it yet," he said. "We will have the proper beats with our publishing team and if I tell you more, they will kill me."
The game's new difficulty is not a harder difficulty, by the way - Rebel Wolves feels Duelist difficulty, without directional attack indicators, is challenging enough. Instead, it's an easier one - the easiest one. It doesn't have a name yet but it effectively replaces the game's current easiest difficulty, Story mode, and takes that name. The existing Story difficulty will be renamed as a result, so Dawnwalker will have five difficulty levels: Story, Story-renamed, Fair, Challenging, and Duelist.
"We will introduce an additional difficulty level," Tomaszkiewicz revealed, "but an easier one, because many people are asking for a more easy difficulty. The Story mode which we have right now will be a different difficulty - we will call it Demanding or something like this - and we will add a new Story mode which will be even easier for people who don't want to experience the combat, they just want to learn the story and go through the game without this gameplay challenge."
Where combat is concerned, targeting and the camera are being worked on, as is that annoying quirk whereby Dawnwalker switches your target when using a stun-like crowd-control ability. Surprisingly enough, this wasn't a bug, but rather something working as Tomaszkiewicz personally intended it. "That's my fault," he said, "because it changed. It worked differently.
"When I was playing in some of the gameplay reviews, I wanted to stun an opponent and then switch to the other one, but because I was locked on him still, I hit him by mistake and took the stun from him, and that's why we made it switch for the other character. But people complain about it, and in the newest patch we will lift off and we will see.
"There will be three hits you need to take off this stun," he added. "We will see how people will react to that because, as I said, it can create another bad feel, but we will see. Maybe people will switch between targets fluently and if they want to just stun, it will be fine, and if they want to stun and hit a few times, it will be also fine. We will see."
Gameplay performance is being addressed - it being a major area of feedback in player reviews on Steam - though there have been incremental hotfix patches already to improve it (as well as things like problematic controller support). As to why it didn't work brilliantly at launch, Tomaszkiewicz cited there being "a lot" of PC hardware combinations, too many to test. But he said: "We're observing this, we're trying to ask people about the hardware, and we are trying to do the fixes."
And he added: "But yes, when you see that the game works well - over 60 FPS - but people still complain that it's not 120, but 90 or 70..." He exhaled here in an exasperated kind of way. "It's like, I understand that but the game is about something else. It's not a shooter - it's not a game where it's so important. But people want to have good performance or performance above good: it's fine. We're working on it and we will still work on it."
As mentioned, making it easier to run away from fights without getting stuck on scenery is also being tackled. This was overlooked because Rebel Wolves devs don't tend to run from fights, heroes that they are, however by watching people stream and reading feedback, they're learning how other people play it. "Right now we're doing the fix where when you run or escape, you will ignore the nav mesh and it will be fluid - it will not be clunky," Tomaszkiewicz said. "We're working on escaping from combat and running in combat and it will be a big change for people."
This extends to enemy animal behaviour, so animals won't "hard-catch" you if you aggravate them while whizzing by in fast mode (wolf form or witch-sprint mode). They will try to hit you, but if they don't manage to, "you are safe and you can run and explore the world freely".
However, what isn't being addressed is enemy sponginess - enemies taking a long time to defeat - because so much of your experience apparently depends upon your character build. "It depends a lot on how you develop your character and what gear you have," Tomaszkiewicz explained. "You can create builds where you're killing them really fast. If you create other builds, they will be more spongey. It's really hard to balance between these because if we decrease the health too much and you create a really strong build, you will one-shot everyone.
"And we had these problems," he said. "That's why we were between those things and tried to compromise between those things. When I played and my human form was [invested] in sword, with some perks in the magic and I had this AoE skill with the crows which was hitting everyone, I was clearing even higher-level opponents really fast. They couldn't do anything. I was too overpowered with this.
"And we didn't change this balance. You can do the builds like this. It depends strongly on you. I know there are some people who don't develop the character and save the perks because they want to do more content, but if you don't spend those perks, the enemies will be more spongy because you don't develop your character."
Tomaszkiewicz said he couldn't remember the rest of the things Rebel Wolves was working on, having already reeled off a fairly long list, but said "there is a lot more which I don't remember right now because it will be a big patch". As to when this patch arrives, he said: "It's quite close. I think that it will be somewhere in the beginning of October. It will be the big patch which will deliver a lot of upgrades for people."
The Blood of Dawnwalker arrived in early September and scored four stars on Eurogamer. I reviewed it and praised its novel time-limiting structure and freeform approach, as well as its enjoyable quests and characters, and its two-sided hero Coen, who's both a witch and vampire. "CD Projekt Red alumni create a familiar dark fantasy adventure, but one with bold and provocative ideas of its own, that's mostly, enormously successful," I wrote in Eurogamer's Dawnwalker review.
Rebel Wolves has already talked quite openly about a desire to do sequels which, with 1m sales already achieved, it seems able to go on and do. The plan is to follow Coen across different eras and locations, but we might not see the return of the divisive time mechanic, intriguingly. "We are also considering and researching some other crazy ideas which can make the RPG genre different to surprise people in the future," Tomaszkiewicz previously said.

item.title: Grand Theft Auto fans are known for a love of speculation and information sleuthing at this point, and this certainly hasn't changed since Rockstar released the extended gameplay preview for Grand Theft Auto 6. The community's current fixation? Whether or not Key West will be in the game. Read more
item.description:
Grand Theft Auto fans are known for a love of speculation and information sleuthing at this point, and this certainly hasn't changed since Rockstar released the extended gameplay preview for Grand Theft Auto 6. The community's current fixation? Whether or not Key West will be in the game.
For months, the most eager among the Grand Theft Auto community have been piecing together whatever clues they can as to what the GTA 6 map looks like. Trailers and leaks in combination have allowed fans to draft a rough idea of what we'll be able to explore come November. However, Key West (or Rockstar's own comedic twist on it) has so far remained unseen.
For those unaware, Key West is the USA's southernmost city, located right on the western tip of a chain of islands known as the Florida Keys. It's a famous spot and a popular tourist destination, leading many to speculate as to how it'll appear in Rockstar's take of the Florida coast.
Questions about Key West's inclusion in GTA 6 have circulated for a while, but the conversation has reignited with the appearance of a map leak which appears to show an early beta version of GTA 6's map. This leak is separate from the CyberLeek posts earlier this summer, which notably did not feature Key West at all. As such, the running theory is that Key West might have been planned but removed later in development.
"I don't see why they'd work so hard doing all the keys and leave out the most important one Key West," wrote Reddit user TheHulk305. "It doesn’t seem like a Rockstar thing to do, especially since we even got the Jersey side of New York in GTA 4." Others speculated that Key West might have been merged with other parts of the Florida Keys. All of this is of course speculation, based upon a map leak which itself could be false.
It'sworth noting, too, that Grand Theft Auto games - while intensely researched and based on real-world locations - are not meant to be one-to-one recreations. Also, just because a leak doesn't show a location doesn't mean it's missing: it could be alluded to in a nearby location or appear significantly smaller than its real world counterpart.
Either way, Grand Theft Auto 6's release is fast approaching, and the ferocious appetite of Grand Theft Auto fans grows ever larger. Key West is not the only notable absence, either, as GTA 6 Online has yet to be announced despite much excitement around it.
Meanwhile, Rockstar is currently in an employment tribunal following the abrupt firing of 31 staff last year, which the former employees argue was an act of union busting. This is still being debated in Scottish employment tribunals, with a verdict set to be released later in October.

item.description:
Metal Gear and Death Stranding creator Hideo Kojima has spoken about a number of topics concerning Sony's sudden shocking decision to back away from publishing his tactical espionage project, Physint. It was a decision made in June, and though Kojima was able to convince Xbox to pick up the Metal Gear successor and continue funding and publishing it, the transition raised a lot of questions.
One of the most obvious questions being: which platforms will the game be available on? Will it be an Xbox exclusive now, or will it still release on PlayStation?
"I don't know the answer to that - that would be a question for Xbox," Kojima told IGN in an interview. "In previous updates from Xbox, I thought that they have this kind of stance where they want to deliver to as many gamers as possible, no matter what the platform is."
Xbox has indeed embraced a multi-platform strategy for several years, but that strategy shifted with new CEO Asha Sharma's arrival at the beginning of the year. Xbox is now once again embracing exclusives, notably confirming recently that Xbox games Gears of War: E-Day and Clockwork Revolution won't be released on PlayStation. However, some games such as Forza Horizon 6 and Fable remain in the works for PS5, so there's hope for Physint.
"I think all of that will be announced at a later time," Kojima added. "I'm not sure yet, and I can't really say."
The other obvious, PlayStation-related question concerns the game's engine. When Kojima left Konami and established his independent Kojima Productions, he spent a lot of time looking for the right engine to build his next project with - the game that would later become Death Stranding.
The engine that won out belonged to Sony; it was Horizon developer Guerrilla Games' internal engine, which the studio gave to Kojima on the condition his team continues adding to it. The engine didn't have a name at that point, but after several modifications, the two parties named it Decima.
So, will Physint share the same engine as the Death Stranding games - Decima? Kojima's answer is complicated. "Well, I haven't really decided yet. I'm still experimenting," he said, when asked if he had to change the game's engine after Sony dropped the project.
"After we decided to team up with Xbox, they said they will give us a lot of technological support. When I went to visit them during the Don Mattrick days, they had so many labs and everything, and they were experimenting on so many things, like state of the art, new, really new, cutting-edge technology.
"I was really surprised," he added. "I was thinking, 'There are so many Doc Browns from Back to the Future here!' So I want to use all this new technology. Anything that I can use, I want to use, and I'm looking forward to teaming up with Xbox, but I really haven't decided about the engine."
It's worth noting that Kojima Productions' next project, the also Xbox-funded OD: Knock, is being developed on Unreal Engine 5, so there's a chance the studio may decide on Epic's popular engine to develop Physint. But considering OD: Knock does not itself have a release target, we maybe waiting a long while yet to see Physint.

item.title: World of Warcraft: Forever's beta has proven exceptionally popular, as 'crazy' numbers of players flock to play this new twist on the beloved MMO. And among Forever's new features is a character naming system that has allowed creative players to get naughty. Read more
item.description:
World of Warcraft: Forever's beta has proven exceptionally popular, as 'crazy' numbers of players flock to play this new twist on the beloved MMO. And among Forever's new features is a character naming system that has allowed creative players to get naughty.
In all other versions of World of Warcraft, characters have one name, so you could call a character "Eurogamer" for example. However in World of Warcraft: Forever, characters have forenames and surnames, so you can call your character "Eurogamer Reader", if you really want to.
This allows for some wonderful roleplaying possibilities, and if you randomly generate a character's name, that's what you get. A nice touch is that these randomly generated fantasy names align with your character's race. The new skyborne elves have wind-themed surnames, for example. However, people love a bit of mischief, and this exploitable two name format has allowed people to create some cheekily named characters.
Naughty names have been screenshotted and posted online ever since the beta launched. One Reddit user - FarKiwi_4882 - shared their collection of noteworthy picks including "Hemorrhoid Man", "TBCisgone Forthisshit", and "Bigpeniss Cok". To which another user, yqozen, responded: "Behold the humankind in all its glory," which seems about right.
Of course, for as long as video game enthusiasts have been given the freedom to express their creative side, they've been quick to get freaky with it. Games like Spore were laden with phallic community creations, and Mythic Quest, a TV show based around game development, grabbed the issue with both hands, addressing the "time to penis" problem in one of its episodes.
Still, this deluge of naughty names has drawn a statement from Blizzard. One player, who complained about being suspended from the WoW: Forever beta, received an official response on the World of Warcraft forums. Customer support rep Vrakthris confirmed that the World of Warcraft naming policies remain present in the beta, and that those reported for having especially naughty names are at risk of having their beta access removed. Blizzard has long relied on player reports to clamp down on such names.
Whether or not this will remain a continuous battle Blizzard has to fight when World of Warcraft: Forever releases in November remains to be seen, but the desire to be crude remains a pathologic urge for us humans. Unless players are keen to report their fellow players for such names, we could very well continue to see such mischief for some time.

item.title: Some Marvel's Wolverine players have claimed their game has been altered to censor aspects of Mystique's lesbian relationship and marriage to Tyger. A number of posts on Reddit and social media appear to show how differently the relationship is referenced compared to the uncensored version. Read more
item.description:
Some Marvel's Wolverine players have claimed their game has been altered to censor aspects of Mystique's lesbian relationship and marriage to Tyger. A number of posts on Reddit and social media appear to show how differently the relationship is referenced compared to the uncensored version.
As spotted by Kotaku, one X user shared a screenshot showing how their game has blurred a framed photo of the pair captured on their wedding day. The photo can still be picked up, but it's entirely blank. A different X user also shared a screenshot of a letter between the couple, which has likewise been entirely blurred so it cannot be read.
The users say the screenshots were captured from the Middle Eastern version of Marvel's Wolverine. Although there's no direct evidence of where these images were taken, this Reddit post also features a clip from the game where the dialogue cuts out whenever "wife" is mentioned in the context of Mystique's relationship. The subtitle further replaces the word with asterisks.
That post is notable as it shows how similar Sony's attempt at censoring the game is to publishers of other media in the Middle East. The tactic of muting certain words or removing them from subtitles is common in films and TV shows shown in the region. This happens when the subject matter has to do with certain aspects of religion, the word "God", or same-sex relationships - all of which are no-nos in many countries in the region. If the entire scene can't be cut, you end up with these modified versions.
Amazon Prime Video's The Boys show is particularly guilty of that, as one example, especially its final season given the subject matter of Homelander's ascent to godhood and the show's references to Jesus Christ. This tactic - at least where streaming shows are concerned - is also not unique to the Middle East; viewers in India have been complaining about it for the last several years.
It's worth mentioning that Mystique's relationship with Tyger hasn't been entirely cut from the game - which would've likely taken a lot more work. Instead, any time the relationship is mentioned in the script or referenced through in-game assets, it's censored in some way. In the uncensored version - without spoiling anything - the two characters' marriage is central to Mystique's part of the story, and indeed the nature of Mystique's friendship with Wolverine.
It's also notable that this is not the first game by Insomniac Games and Sony to be censored in certain parts of the world. Marvel's Spider-Man 2 was modified prior to its release in Saudi Arabia to remove LGBTQ+ references, such as the Pride Flag and a side mission featuring a gay couple.
Saudi Arabia's General Authority for Media Regulation, the country's media rating board, announced in September 2023 the game had been classified "after the publishing studio approved the requested modifications" albeit without saying what those modifications were.
Though a different publisher, many within EA have raised concerns about the company's recent acquisition by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF), and how it could change the publisher's identity. EA has long had LGBTQ+ characters in its games and tackled themes of same-sex romance on many occasions. The Sims series is especially beloved by many in the LGBTQ+ community for its progressive treatment of characters and for recognising same-sex relationships, and there's a real worry a Saudi-owned EA won't be allowed to do any of that.

item.title: UPDATE 22ND SEPTEMBER: Former NetEase studio investor and Rebel Wolves board director Simon Zhu has revealed the "entire budget" of The Blood of Dawnwalker as $45m, and said that: "In Poland, that budget is AAA." Read more
item.description:
UPDATE 22ND SEPTEMBER: Former NetEase studio investor and Rebel Wolves board director Simon Zhu has revealed the "entire budget" of The Blood of Dawnwalker as $45m, and said that: "In Poland, that budget is AAA."
In a post on LinkedIn, Zhu said: "In 2022, we funded the project in full at the outset - $45 million, the entire budget - so Konrad would never have to worry about money and could focus on getting the game finished and out. (The Fed was already signaling rate hikes. The party was about to end.) In Poland, that budget is AAA."
Zhu's post went on to praise the game's success and highlight a few key reasons for it, such as games being "made by people", the importance of clear leadership, and having people there to "strip away the distractions and solve the problems inside and outside game development" - people like Zhu, it sounds like.
What does Zhu know? Well, in their role as studio partner for NetEase they've worked on the boards of many game companies, including Quantic Dream, Thatgamecompany, Behaviour Interactive, Devolver, Kepler and more. But as of a year ago they've started their own thing: a funding group and game partner called GreaterThanGroup, which is - most notably - the partner for Casey Hudson's hotly anticipated new Star Wars RPG Fate of the Old Republic.
ORIGINAL STORY 21ST SEPTEMBER: Polish developer Rebel Wolves has revealed the budget for dark fantasy vampire role-playing game The Blood of Dawnwalker, and it's lower than expected, aligning it more closely with a double-A production than a triple-A blockbuster.
In an interview with Bloomberg, studio co-founder and game director Konrad Tomaszkiewicz revealed Dawnwalker's budget as $40 million, which is a far cry from even the budget of a fairly linear blockbuster like 007 First Light, which reportedly cost $200m to make (though there were hefty licensing fees and high profile actors' wages to pay in that case).
A more pertinent comparison, perhaps, is to CD Projekt Red's The Witcher 3, which Tomaszkiewicz directed and which Dawnwalker is so alike. That game cost $80m to make, though a large chunk of that figure reportedly went on marketing. Still, Tomaszkiewicz has often talked about the two games' productions being broadly equivalent in scope, which they don't quite appear to be; and if you factor in that The Witcher 3 cost $80m more than a decade ago, the gap widens further still.
Despite a lower budget, Rebel Wolves - a studio 29 percent owned by Chinese behemoth Tencent - does show triple-A ambition in Dawnwalker, and occasionally realises it, though there is a pervading sense the visuals aren't quite cutting edge and the world is sometimes stretched thin, becoming repetitive.
But what Dawnwalker lacks in that regard it makes up for in originality, with a bold take on RPG structure that does away with a main quest and leaves your adventure up to you, while limiting the time you have available for it. Dawnwalker is exactly the kind of risk-taking game former PlayStation boss Shawn Layden said our industry is in desperate need of, when he talked about bringing double-A games back.
I gave The Blood of Dawnwalker four stars in our review. "CD Projekt Red alumni create a familiar dark fantasy adventure," I wrote, "but one with bold and provocative ideas of its own, that's mostly, enormously successful."

item.title: Microsoft has filed a patent for a system that allows PC and Xbox games to serve advertisements during game sessions, seemingly without disrupting gameplay. Read more
item.description:
The patent, published 3rd September in the US (via Respawn First), is described as "context aware" and relies on what it calls an "ad credit" system. It works by recognising "trigger events" in a game, which then cause an advert to be shown.
The credit system, incidentally, assigns players chunks of ad-free time, and when each block of time expires, the game shows promoted content.
Although the application of such technology remains a mystery, Microsoft has indicated in the past it is exploring different ways for players to access its software, services and hardware. Indeed, Microsoft has already started testing an ad-based tier of Xbox cloud gaming.
A recent rumour said the company is working on shaking up Xbox Game Pass tiers yet again, as well, this time to introduce a cheaper, ad-supported tier - a first for the subscription service. Microsoft did not directly deny the rumour, saying it "regularly tests different Game Pass offerings and looks at what works best for players in different markets".

item.title: Zach Cregger's quirky new Resident Evil film is a big success, recording the best opening weekend for a Resident Evil film ever. Read more
item.description:
Zach Cregger's quirky new Resident Evil film is a big success, recording the best opening weekend for a Resident Evil film ever.
Cregger's Resident Evil pulled in $108.3 (£93m) globally during its opening weekend, Deadline reported, split $60m in the US market and $48.3m internationally. That's more than Cregger's hit horror Weapons ($70m) and comfortably higher than any of the previous Resident Evil films. It's apparently the second-best result for a horror film this year behind the sensation that was Backrooms ($118m).
Incidentally, the first Jovovich Resident Evil film, released in 2002, made $102.9m in total, Deadline noted, so Cregger's film has already beaten it. 2016's Resident Evil: The Final Chapter has a lifetime total of approximately $312m (half of that apparently coming from China).
Cregger's comedic approach to the Resident Evil series divided opinion in the run up to release. He decided to opt for a non-heroic approach, rejecting roles for famed series characters Leon S. Kennedy and the Redfields, and preferring instead to tell a more everyday story through the eyes of medical delivery driver Bryan (played by actor Austin Abrams) who bumbles his way through an extraordinarily bad day on the job.
I watched Resident Evil at the weekend and really liked it. By using comedy, Cregger has found a new approach, which actually affords the film some surprisingly unsettling and shocking moments. It's much harder to predict.
There's plenty of horror here, by the way, alongside the absurd comedy, but there's also a much more grounded and 'easier to relate to' story, as Bryan fumbles with guns and ammo and nerves, and blurts out reactions closely mirrored - in my case - by the audience's thoughts.
Game-maker Capcom is currently working on a remake of old Resident Evil game Code: Veronica, which it's calling simply Resident Evil Veronica, which is due for release next year.

item.title: If you've been hungering for something gothic as we inch towards October, the scariest month of the year, then you're in luck. Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is getting a demo you'll be able to sink your fangs into soon. Read more
item.description:
If you've been hungering for something gothic as we inch towards October, the scariest month of the year, then you're in luck. Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is getting a demo you'll be able to sink your fangs into soon.
Developer Evil Empire - known for its work on Dead Cells and the similarly styled Rogue Prince of Persia - has announced its Belmont's Curse demo arrives on 1st October, coming to Switch, PS5, Xbox Series X/S, and PC. Those who chose to download it can play through the entire first chapter, with any progress made carrying over to the game's full release on the 14th October. Expect 60FPS across all platforms except for the Switch, where 30FPS is the target.
This demo chapter is the same portion of Belmont's Curse experienced by previewers earlier this year, including me! In Eurogamer's own preview, I came away thoroughly impressed by what I played: Rose Belmont's adventure seemed to be a fantastic blend of old and new action-platformer trends. Whether or not the rest of the game stands up to this stellar first impression is something we'll all find out next month.
Belmont's Curse is set to be the first of multiple Castlevania projects coming from Konami, though what exactly else the company has in store for the series remains a mystery for now. It's clear that since the popular Netflix adaptation reignited interest in the series there's been a newfound push to revive Castlevania. One can only hope Konami manages to do as well with this classic series as they have with Silent Hill, with Silent Hill: Townfall standing strong as yet another solid entry for horror fans.

item.description:
Marvel's Wolverine has received a hotfix update that addresses one of the core features in the game many people have an issue with: scent trails. These are represented on screen by a gassy, bright blue line, and they're used by Wolverine to locate his next mission objective and to find collectibles in the world.
This patch, version 01.001.005, doesn't remove the scent trails but it does change their opacity so they're less pronounced. The same also extends to audio sense indicators, toning them down.
In the blog post announcing the hotfix, developer Insomniac Games said it "continues to evaluate ways to further improve senses", and that it's exploring offering the ability to toggle them off entirely in a future update.
Dubbed "fart gas" by some players, the feature has been widely mocked online. Even before the game's launch, fans asked for a toggle to turn it off once it became clear they found the scents distracting.
Insomniac has also addressed some game crashes, which apparently "a small percentage of players" were experiencing.
Although Sony has yet to announce any official sales figures for Marvel's Wolverine, early estimates put it at 1.9 million copies. This includes digital pre-orders as well as launch day sales, amounting to around $130m (~£97m) in revenue for Sony so far. Incidentally, 22.9 percent of sales came from the physical version, which is lower than the developer's Marvel's Spider-Man 2 game, with 35 percent.
In Eurogamer's Marvel's Wolverine review, Chris Tapsell was underwhelmed by the game's outdated, old-school design, which was partly redeemed by its likeable character work.
If online controversies and mixed reviews haven't deterred you from playing the game, consider bookmarking Eurogamer's Marvel's Wolverine guide for general tips, collectible and suit locations as well as a full walkthrough.

item.title: As I watch the credits roll on Silent Hill: Townfall, it's hard to believe this is the same series that had, until just a few years ago, been neglected into near-irrelevance. Like 2025's excellent Silent Hill f, Townfall is a fascinating thing; a game of bold creative swings that's part inversion, subversion, and evolution of the near-three-decade survival horror series, charting its own idiosyncratic path while still feeling entirely Silent Hill.
